passage:
Neelam keeps the accounts for the milk cooperative in a small town by the canal. From eight each morning, farmers start calling about payments, and both the office phone and her own mobile ring.
Swati, the new clerk, watched her first week in awe. Neelam put the mobile on silent, turned it screen down and wrote on the slate by the door: "Calls answered at 11 and 3." Then she worked on the ledger for ninety minutes without looking up. At eleven she returned every call in one go, then walked to the tea stall for ten minutes.
"Doesn't anyone get angry?" Swati asked.
"At first. Now they know when I'll call. And the ledger has no mistakes, so payments go out on time."
By four, Neelam's work was done. Swati's, answered call by call, was not.

qa.q: What did Neelam write on the slate by the door?
qa.a: Neelam wrote "Calls answered at 11 and 3."

qa.q: Why was Swati in awe during the first week?
qa.a: Swati seemed amazed that Neelam could leave phones unanswered for ninety minutes and still finish everything, when answering each call had felt like the only way.

qa.q: What could Swati borrow from Neelam's routine?
qa.a: Swati could set fixed call times, silence the mobile during ledger work and take a short break afterwards, instead of answering call by call.

qa.q: How do the farmers experience Neelam's call times?
qa.a: Some got angry at first, but now they know when she'll call, and their payments arrive on time with no mistakes.

grounding: It shows a young cooperative accountant who works in a single focused block, silences her phone, batches calls and then rests.

passage:
On Tuesday mornings, Santiago's small design studio in Valencia smells of coffee and the bakery downstairs. At nine he closes his email, puts his phone in a drawer with notifications off and sets a kitchen timer for fifty minutes. Then he works on one poster, nothing else.
Kofi, at the desk opposite, used to tease him. Kofi keeps chat, mail and three projects open and answers everything within a minute. "You're so slow to reply," Kofi said.
When the timer rings, Santiago answers all his messages in one fifteen-minute burst, then walks around the block. By lunch he has sent a finished poster to the client. Kofi is still halfway through two.
The next week, Kofi borrowed the kitchen timer.

qa.q: How long does Santiago set the kitchen timer for?
qa.a: Santiago sets the kitchen timer for fifty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Kofi think Santiago was slow?
qa.a: Replying within a minute feels efficient to Kofi, so Santiago's delayed answers looked slow, even though Santiago finished first.

qa.q: What choice did Kofi make the following week, and why is it a good start?
qa.a: Kofi borrowed the kitchen timer, a simple first step towards single-task blocks after seeing a finished poster beat two half-done ones.

qa.q: How might the client see Santiago's way of working?
qa.a: The client gets a finished poster by lunch and one clear batch of replies, which probably feels more reliable than instant but scattered answers.

grounding: It shows a young designer who works in timed single-task blocks with notifications off, batches messages and then takes a walk.

passage:
At the university exam office, results for three departments were due on Friday. Asif, the youngest officer, stuck a note on the monitor: "10 to 12: marks only. 12 to 12:30: emails. 2 to 4: marks only. 4:30: tea." The phone went into the desk drawer on silent, and the email tab stayed closed.
Karthik, at the next desk, kept everything open and replied to each ping. "You'll miss something urgent," Karthik warned.
Nothing came that couldn't wait ninety minutes. By Thursday afternoon, Asif had entered and checked two departments with zero errors. Karthik had half of one done and was re-entering a column mixed up during a phone call.
On Friday Karthik asked to copy the note. Asif printed it twice.

qa.q: What did the note on Asif's monitor set aside for 12 to 12:30?
qa.a: The note set aside 12 to 12:30 for emails.

qa.q: Why did Karthik worry that Asif would miss something urgent?
qa.a: Karthik felt that answering every ping at once was the responsible way to work, so a closed email tab seemed risky.

qa.q: Which choice let Asif finish two departments with zero errors?
qa.a: Splitting the day into marks-only and email-only times, with the phone in the drawer, meant fewer switches and fewer mix-ups.

qa.q: What is it like for Karthik re-entering the mixed-up column?
qa.a: Karthik probably feels frustrated and behind, redoing work lost during a call, which is why the note suddenly looks worth copying.

grounding: It shows a young officer who works in single-task blocks, silences the phone and batches emails, finishing better work sooner.

passage:
Hi Zubin,
You asked how I finish translation jobs so fast now. It isn't speed. It's fewer switches.
Here's my day. From nine to eleven I translate one document, only that. Notifications off, chat closed, phone in the other room. At eleven I open email and messages and answer everything in one go, maybe twenty minutes. Then a proper break: I walk to the tea stall and back without my phone. Then another block, on a different document.
Last year I kept the chat open "just in case" and jumped at every ping. I thought I was being responsive. My work had silly errors and my evenings were gone. Now I finish by five, and not one client has complained about waiting till eleven.
Try one block tomorrow. Just one.
Ritu

qa.q: What does Ritu do at eleven?
qa.a: Opens email and messages and answers everything in one go, maybe twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Ritu once feel keeping the chat open was the right thing?
qa.a: Jumping at every ping felt responsive and professional, so Ritu didn't see how much it was costing in errors and lost evenings.

qa.q: What single step does Ritu suggest Zubin try first, and why start small?
qa.a: One focused block tomorrow; trying just one lets Zubin feel the difference without changing a whole working day at once.

qa.q: How have Ritu's clients been affected by the change?
qa.a: They get fewer errors and haven't complained about waiting until eleven, so the focused blocks seem to have helped them too.

grounding: A translator explains working in single-task blocks with notifications off, batched messages and real breaks, and how it improved the work.

passage: Kiran, since your show is about work habits, here's mine. I'm Baljeet, I prepare accounts for small shops, and a year ago I was the queen of multitasking. Three spreadsheets open, phone on the desk, answering every client call in the middle of an entry. I felt busy all day. Then I added a customer's cash twice in a year-end statement, and the shop owner found it before I did. That stung. So I tried blocks. Ninety minutes on one client's books, phone silent, email closed. Then half an hour for all the calls and messages together. Then I get up, stretch, drink water, look out of the window. The first week felt strangely slow. By the second, I was finishing a client in a day instead of three. Turns out I wasn't doing three things at once. I was doing three things badly.

qa.q: What mistake did Baljeet make in the year-end statement?
qa.a: Added a customer's cash twice.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when the shop owner found the mistake first?
qa.a: It stung; she felt embarrassed and shaken, which pushed her to change how she worked 😔

qa.q: Which part of Baljeet's new routine makes the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Ninety-minute blocks on one client's books with the phone silent, because without switching she finishes a client in a day instead of three.

qa.q: How might the shop owner see Baljeet's work after the change?
qa.a: The owner would likely trust her more again, getting accurate books faster after that first worrying mistake.

grounding: A young accountant describes moving from constant switching to focused blocks, batched calls and breaks, and getting better work done faster.

passage: I've shared a desk cluster with Nirmala at the design studio in Bengaluru for a year, and I still can't fully explain her. I'm Elizabeth. From nine to eleven every morning, Nirmala puts on her big headphones, closes her mail, and props up a little card that says 'Deep work till 11'. Her phone goes face down. We learned not to disturb her. At eleven she opens everything at once and answers all the messages in about twenty minutes. Then she takes a walk outside. Afternoons are the same: one more block. I used to think she was being antisocial. Then I noticed her designs were always done first, with fewer revisions than anyone's. I don't know how it feels inside her head. But last month I made my own card.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's little card say?
qa.a: 'Deep work till 11'.

qa.q: What might Nirmala feel during her morning block, as far as Elizabeth can tell?
qa.a: Nirmala seems calm and absorbed in one task, though Elizabeth admits not knowing how it feels inside her head.

qa.q: Which parts of Nirmala's routine make her work faster?
qa.a: Single-task blocks with notifications off, answering all messages together at eleven, and a walk to rest.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth's view of Nirmala change over the year?
qa.a: Elizabeth went from thinking Nirmala was antisocial to admiring her results and making a card of her own.

grounding: Shows, through a colleague's eyes, a young professional working in single-task blocks, batching messages and resting.

passage:
Monday. Jyoti, a junior analyst, answered forty-three messages, sat through two meetings with her laptop open, and started four reports. She finished none. At eight in the evening she was still at her desk, head pounding.
Wednesday. She tried an experiment. Two ninety-minute blocks, one report each, notifications off, phone in her drawer. She checked messages only at 11:30 and 4:00, all at once. Between blocks she walked round the office car park.
The following Friday. Both reports had been finished by Thursday afternoon, with fewer errors than usual. Hrithik, her manager, asked what had changed. "I stopped switching," Jyoti said. "It turns out the switching was the work I was doing all day."

qa.q: How many messages did Jyoti answer on Monday?
qa.a: Forty-three.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel at eight on Monday evening?
qa.a: Jyoti felt exhausted and frustrated, head pounding, with four reports started and none finished.

qa.q: What did Jyoti's experiment involve, and why did it work?
qa.a: Ninety-minute single-report blocks with notifications off, messages batched at two set times, and walks in between, so fewer switches meant better work in less time.

qa.q: Why might Hrithik have asked what had changed?
qa.a: Hrithik noticed the reports came in early with fewer errors, which surprised him.

grounding: Shows a young analyst moving from constant switching to single-task blocks, batched messages and short rests, with better work in less time.

passage: Deepak, you've answered emails through our whole conversation. Let old Avni tell you what I learned at twenty-four, when I started as a translator at the publishing house in Kolkata. I had a phone that rang all day, a pile of manuscripts, and a boss who expected replies within minutes. I was translating and taking calls and checking proofs all at once, and I was always behind. One day my mentor, Mr Ganguly, locked my phone in his drawer from ten to twelve. I was furious. In those two hours I translated eleven pages, more than in the whole previous week. After that I kept those hours sacred: one manuscript, door closed. I returned calls after lunch, all together, then walked to the tea stall. I've translated forty books since. Close the email, Deepak.

qa.q: How many pages did young Avni translate in the two locked hours?
qa.a: Eleven pages.

qa.q: How did young Avni feel when Mr Ganguly locked the phone away, and afterwards?
qa.a: Avni felt furious at first, then amazed and relieved at doing more in two hours than in the whole previous week.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Avni's story, and what routine followed?
qa.a: Mr Ganguly locking the phone away; afterwards Avni kept two sacred hours for one manuscript, returned calls together after lunch, then walked to the tea stall.

qa.q: Why might Mr Ganguly have locked the phone in his drawer?
qa.a: Mr Ganguly probably saw Avni constantly switching and falling behind, and wanted to show what focus could do.

grounding: Shows a young translator discovering single-task blocks, batched calls and rest, and passing the lesson on.

passage:
Pradeep had a client report due by five, his daughter's school had called twice, and the office printer was broken. It was already noon.

His colleague Karthik watched him put his phone on silent, close his email, and set a timer for fifty minutes.

"What if your daughter's school calls again?"

"I've told my wife to call twice if it's urgent. That comes through."

He wrote without stopping till the timer rang. Then ten minutes: he answered all his messages in one go, called the school back, and made tea. Then another fifty-minute block.

At 4:15 he sent the report. Karthik, still halfway through his own, sighed. "How?"

"Fewer switches," Pradeep said. "That's all."

qa.q: How long was each of Pradeep's work blocks?
qa.a: Fifty minutes.

qa.q: How does Pradeep seem to feel while working in blocks?
qa.a: He seems calm and in control, trusting that urgent calls will still reach him, so he can focus fully.

qa.q: What in Pradeep's approach could Karthik copy?
qa.a: Karthik could silence notifications, work in timed single-task blocks and answer messages together during short breaks.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel when Pradeep finishes early?
qa.a: Karthik probably feels a bit envious and curious, wondering how to work the same way.

grounding: Under pressure, a professional works in single-task blocks, silences alerts and batches messages, finishing faster.

passage:
Every morning at nine, Kashish closed the door of her small room at the architecture firm in Pune. Notifications off, one drawing on the screen.

Her new colleague Alka found it odd. "Don't you check messages?"

"At eleven and at three," Kashish said. "All at once."

Alka tried to work like everyone else, with chat open and email pinging. By lunch she had started three drawings and finished none.

Kashish had finished the first floor plan and gone for a short walk.

"I used to work like you," Kashish told her. "I thought I was fast. I was just busy."

The next morning, Alka closed her chat for an hour. It felt strange at first. By eleven, she had a whole elevation done.

qa.q: At what times does Kashish check messages?
qa.a: At eleven and at three.

qa.q: How might Alka have felt by lunch with three drawings started and none finished?
qa.a: She probably felt frustrated and a bit discouraged, working hard but getting little done.

qa.q: Which of Kashish's habits made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Checking messages only at set times, because it cut the switching that kept breaking her focus.

qa.q: What would change for Alka if she kept working in focused blocks?
qa.a: She would likely finish more drawings in less time and feel less scattered.

grounding: A productive professional works in single-task blocks, silences notifications, batches messages and rests.

"Anirban, how are you already done with the budget sheet?"

"Started at nine. Stopped at ten-thirty."

"I started at nine too," Nitin said. "But the team chat, the emails, two calls..."

"I turned all that off. Put a note on my status: back at ten-thirty."

"And if something's urgent?"

"They can call. Nobody did."

"Then what?"

"Then I replied to everything in one go. Took fifteen minutes. Then I got coffee and walked around the block."

"You walked? In the middle of the day?"

"That's why I'm not fried by three."

Nitin looked at his own screen, twelve tabs open, and closed eleven.

passage:
A year ago I was the fastest replier in my office. I'm Shreya, and I answered every email within two minutes and every chat within ten seconds. Then my manager, Sabina, asked how the big report was coming along. It wasn't. I'd been working all day, and it was still on page two.
So I tried something that felt lazy at first. Mornings from nine to eleven: one task only, notifications off, phone in a drawer. Then half an hour to answer everything at once. Then another block. Then a real lunch, away from my desk.
The first week I was anxious that people would think I'd disappeared. Nobody did. The report was done in four days instead of three weeks.
Now I work in blocks, check messages three times a day and leave at six. I get more done in less time, and I'm less tired. The switching was what had been eating my day.

qa.q: What hours is Shreya's first focused block?
qa.a: Nine to eleven in the morning.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel in the first week of working in blocks?
qa.a: Shreya felt anxious that people would think Shreya had disappeared, though nobody did.

qa.q: What does Shreya's routine include, and why does it work?
qa.a: Single-task blocks with notifications off, messages batched three times a day and a real lunch, so fewer switches mean better work in less time.

qa.q: How might Sabina see the change in Shreya's work?
qa.a: Sabina would likely be pleased and relieved, seeing the report finished in four days instead of three weeks.

grounding: Shows a young professional who moves to single-task blocks, silenced notifications and batched messages, and does better work in less time.

passage:
Manager's note, quarterly review. Written by Parul, team manager.
In January, Varun told me he wanted to try working in focus blocks: two ninety-minute blocks a day with chat and email closed, messages answered in batches at twelve and four, and a proper break between.
At first I was worried clients would complain about slower replies. I watched closely.
No complaints came. Varun's code reviews dropped from twelve errors a week to three. He finished the payment module two weeks early. He says he goes home less tired.
Two others on the team have now asked to try the same thing.
What I did next: I've made 10 to 11:30 quiet time for the whole team, with no meetings, and we're trying it for a month.

qa.q: How many errors a week did Varun's code reviews drop to?
qa.a: Varun's code reviews dropped from twelve errors a week to three.

qa.q: How does Varun feel at the end of the day now?
qa.a: Varun feels less tired going home, after working in focused blocks.

qa.q: Why did the focus blocks improve Varun's work?
qa.a: Two ninety-minute blocks with chat and email closed and messages batched meant fewer switches, fewer errors and faster work.

qa.q: How did Parul feel at first about Varun's plan?
qa.a: Parul felt worried that clients would complain about slower replies, then reassured when none did.

grounding: Shows, in a manager's note, a young professional whose single-task blocks and batched messages lead to better work in less time.

passage:
Monday, 7 p.m.
Day one of the experiment Kiran suggested. Kiran swears by it: work on one thing at a time, notifications off, check messages only at 11, 2 and 5, and take a real break after each block.
Morning block, 9:30 to 11: just the tender document. I felt jumpy for the first twenty minutes, reaching for my phone every time a thought popped up. Then something happened. I got into it. By eleven I had written more than I usually manage in a whole day.
At eleven I answered 23 messages in fifteen minutes. None had been urgent.
Afternoon block: the budget sheet. Same thing.
At four I walked to the tea stall without my phone and actually tasted the tea.
Tired, but a good tired. Tomorrow, same plan.
Pranav
